description_full: Applied Materials, Inc. provides materials engineering solutions, equipment, services, and software to the semiconductor and related industries in the United States, China, Korea, Taiwan, Japan, Southeast Asia, Europe, and internationally. The company operates through Semiconductor Systems and Applied Global Services (AGS) segments. The Semiconductor Systems segment includes semiconductor capital equipment to enable materials engineering steps, including etch, rapid thermal processing, deposition, chemical mechanical planarization, metrology and inspection, wafer packaging, and ion implantation. The AGS segment offers integrated solutions to optimize equipment and fab performance and productivity comprising spares, upgrades, services, and 200 millimeter and other equipment and factory automation software for semiconductor and other products. It serves manufacturers of semiconductor wafers and chips, and other electronic devices. Applied Materials, Inc. was incorporated in 1967 and is headquartered in Santa Clara, California.

financial_summary: Applied Materials, Inc. is a mega-cap technology business with a $264.0B market cap on $28.4B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and +11% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory. Operating margins are expanding by +2.3pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 45% against a 12% cost of capital — a 33-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 44%.

The business throws off $5.7B in free cash flow — roughly 20 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.14× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 31× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.3% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.
